name: Adam Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a tyre-curing press crew and check the first tread after a mould change. I have a two-year technical diploma and am one of the best at finding a bad vent from the press sound. I like showing apprentices a safe check, and I dislike a hot press opened to meet a rushed target.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Farah works in home care and our grown children have homes of their own. Premium pay lifts my wage above the usual operator rate, we have sixteen months saved, a mortgage and plenty of similar tyre plants nearby. I use AI now and then to group downtime notes, but the signed heat record governs a cure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the tyre crew that small software gains are fine if nobody forgets the first cured tyre. A clean schedule does not tell you whether the mould vent blocked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the curing presses and can hear an uneven closing stroke, but I still show the apprentice how to check the first tyre. My partner Farah works in home care, our grown children have homes, and sixteen months saved plus my premium wage cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the press shift and inspect the first tread under a good light. I use AI now and then to group downtime notes, but would check the handwritten temperature record; I would pay a little extra mortgage principal from each new full wage after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be calm. I like a Saturday when the phone stays quiet and Farah and I can cook for the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a blocked vent do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It leaves a tiny bubble in the tread where air should have escaped. I stop the press and clear the vent before another tyre comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does AI set the curing time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I use it occasionally for notes, and the signed heat record controls the machine.

feel: **Calm** with current work and strong household finances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can order materials faster, while a robot taking hot tyres from a press needs cautious testing. I would try a new heat-trend chart after the fitter proves it on old cycles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farah’s home-care work and my skilled press role look sound over the next few years. A faster loading robot may change later rosters, but I do not expect my own pay to fall soon; I want measured evidence before buying trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request an offered paid trial on a cold, isolated training press with the fitter present and old cure records. If approved, I would learn the new AI heat-trend chart against actual temperature logs; I would keep my paid shifts and tell the union what the trial showed before anyone agreed a live change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about the changing floor, not afraid of the next wage slip. A nice graph can be wrong about a hot tyre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let the chart set a live cycle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after an offered paid guarded practice slot and the fitter’s sign-off. I would still inspect the first cured tyre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. This is the plant’s machine, and its training must happen on paid time with proper guards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2028 finds me sixty, and capable tyre-handling robots around 2031 find me sixty-three. The ordering desk changes first; the hot presses need hands for a while longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot could reduce our curing crew and perhaps my own shifts by 2031. Sixteen months saved and many nearby tyre plants buy time, but Farah’s care wage cannot carry the mortgage forever if my pay stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request dated staffing plans and postpone buying the camper we have discussed. If my shifts were actually cut, I would apply for posted reachable curing or inspection roles only where net pay after travel covers housing and food, and wait for a real offer and start date before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a possible loss of work, with some control over the search. A camper is easy to delay; a mortgage is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I enjoy teaching the line and planned to work toward seventy if health permits. I would need verified household income before choosing an earlier last day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your children fund the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes. I would ask for a lift to an interview if needed, not their wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three, and capable press robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years gives time to offer a proper mould-maintenance qualification to people who know the heat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I understand a blocked vent, but maintenance work needs recognised certification and supervised practice on a cold, isolated press. I will not lose full paid shifts for an unoffered course or take a role that pays too little after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid curing shift and ask the union to seek a funded course during paid hours. If offered an actual place with a qualified fitter supervising guarded cold-press practice and a posted reachable maintenance role at bill-covering net pay after travel, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for the role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about later robots but comfortable checking a real opportunity. I can teach a new operator and still admit when I need a fitter beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would lock out the press and show me a vent replacement on a cold training mould. I would need the actual offered paid place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If no place opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and compare posted tyre jobs if hours fell. I would not pay for a private certificate merely to look prepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight, and capable tyre robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. I had meant to keep teaching the curing line to about seventy if health and pay allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our sixteen-month reserve does not itself fund retirement. I do not know what any pension will pay, what Farah’s future care hours will be, or whether the mortgage will be cleared by seventy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep paid curing shifts and pay extra mortgage principal from fresh full wages after bills. In the first year after 2036, if still safely employed, I would keep working and check actual pay and health; I would request retirement and mortgage figures, then leave factory work at my planned seventy only if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs, otherwise continue safe paid work or apply after cuts for posted reachable work with bill-covering net pay after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about distant robots while our current finances are sound. I want to hand over the line because I chose to, not because I guessed at a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would seventy be earlier retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that is the age I have been aiming for. I would leave earlier only if actual figures and health made that sensible, but I am not planning it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children help with costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes. I can teach them what the job taught me, but not put their wages into our retirement calculation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because press robots around 2031 could reduce our curing crew while I still intend to earn wages. Written staffing plans, offered funded paid guarded maintenance training and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who inspected the first tyre after a mould change. A good heat chart cannot feel a bubble in the tread.
